segments.title: HMS Foxglove's three-decade Acacia-class career
segments.summary: HMS Foxglove was an Acacia-class Royal Navy minesweeping sloop launched in 1915 and scrapped in 1946.
segments.body: HMS Foxglove was an Acacia-class minesweeping sloop of the Royal Navy. Barclay Curle launched her in Glasgow in 1915, and she commissioned that year. Minesweeping was the class's primary purpose. Foxglove's career extended across both world wars, ending with her scrapping in 1946.

evidence.note: The transcript identifies Foxglove as an Acacia-class Royal Navy minesweeping sloop, gives her 1915 launch at Barclay Curle in Glasgow and commission that year, dates her scrapping to 1946, and states the class's primary minesweeping purpose.

segments.title: Foxglove's compact hull and proportions
segments.summary: Foxglove displaced about 1,200 tons, with length measurements of 250 feet and 262 feet 6 inches, a 33-foot beam, and a 12-foot draft.
segments.body: Foxglove displaced roughly 1,200 tons. The length figures given are 250 feet (76 metres) at the shortest measurement and 262 feet 6 inches (80.1 metres) at the longest. Neither bow nor stern is described as especially pronounced. Her beam was 33 feet (10 metres), and her draft was about 12 feet (3.7 metres).

evidence.note: The transcript gives 1,200 tons, lengths of 250 feet (76 metres) and 262 feet 6 inches (80.1 metres), a 33-foot (10-metre) beam, a corrected draft of 12 feet (3.7 metres), and the limited projection of her bow and stern.

segments.title: Foxglove's armament changed during service
segments.summary: The Acacia-class design specified two 12-pounders and two 3-pounders, while Foxglove's reported service fits included 4-inch guns and additional 3-pounders.
segments.body: The Acacia-class design called for two 12-pounder guns of 76 mm calibre and two 3-pounders of 47 mm calibre. Foxglove did not necessarily carry that nominal battery throughout her career. At several points she appears to have been fitted with 4-inch guns and additional 3-pounders. The class specification alone cannot establish Foxglove's armament at a particular date.

evidence.note: The transcript specifies two 12-pounders (76 mm) and two 3-pounders (47 mm), then contrasts that design battery with apparent four-inch-gun fits and additional 3-pounders during service.

segments.title: From World War I minesweeping to wider wartime service
segments.summary: Foxglove spent about two years sweeping mines before moving into broader fighting duties in 1917.
segments.body: Foxglove's early World War I work followed the Acacia class's primary minesweeping role. She spent about two years in that role before her duties changed in 1917. She then undertook broader fighting service. No individual operation or engagement is named in this account of the change.

evidence.note: The transcript says Foxglove performed minesweeping duties until 1917 before being turned to broader war-fighting work.

segments.title: China Station rescue work with HMS Carlisle
segments.summary: On the China Station, Foxglove helped HMS Carlisle rescue survivors from the grounded SS Hong Moh in 1921.
segments.body: Foxglove served on the China Station during the 1920s. On 3 March 1921, she took part in efforts to assist passengers from SS Hong Moh. The ship had grounded on the White Rocks off Lamock Island in China. Foxglove worked alongside the C-class cruiser HMS Carlisle. Together, the two Royal Navy ships rescued 221 survivors.

evidence.note: The transcript places Foxglove on the China Station during the 1920s, dates her rescue involvement to 3 March 1921, locates the grounding at the White Rocks off Lamock Island in China, and credits Foxglove and HMS Carlisle jointly with rescuing 221 survivors. The additional place name rendered as 'swathal' at 2:21 is unclear and is omitted from the public note.

segments.title: Dive-bomb damage and wartime support service
segments.summary: German dive bombers damaged Foxglove off the Isle of Wight in July 1940, but she remained afloat and served out the war in support roles.
segments.body: German aircraft dive-bombed and damaged Foxglove off the Isle of Wight in July 1940, ending her active wartime contribution early. The ship remained afloat and was converted into an accommodation and base ship. She then served as a harbour guard ship at Londonderry, Northern Ireland, for the rest of the war. Her earlier overseas service included the China Station and the Mediterranean, although no specific Mediterranean duties are described. Foxglove was scrapped in 1946 after a long career that continued through support duties following the attack.

evidence.note: The transcript describes dive-bomb damage off the Isle of Wight, conversion to accommodation and base-ship roles, harbour guard service at Londonderry, and 1946 scrapping.
The closing remarks mention China Station and Mediterranean service, note that active World War II work ended early in July 1940, and judge the ship a valuable build.
